summary: Gives guidance for choosing policies on how values in a protocol namespace are assigned, and the text that authors must put in an IANA Considerations section. It helps keep protocol numbers and names well managed. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 5226.

eli5.summary: Some protocols need lists of numbers handed out fairly, like seat numbers at a theater. This tells authors how to write down the rules for handing them out.

questions: how to write an iana considerations section
subtitle: How protocol specifications should document the rules for managing IANA registries.

tldr.problem: Many IETF protocol specifications create registries of numbers and values that IANA must manage, but RFC authors often failed to specify clear policies for how new values should be assigned.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2434 provides guidelines for authors on what must be written in an IANA Considerations section, explains different assignment policies (first-come-first-served, expert review, standards action, etc.), and describes how IANA should handle registrations.
tldr.outcome: The IETF now has consistent guidance for documenting protocol registries, ensuring IANA can make fair and consistent assignments. RFC 2434 was replaced by RFC 5226 with expanded guidance.

today: RFC 2434 is a Best Current Practice published in October 1998. It was updated by RFC 3692 (April 1st procedures) and obsoleted by RFC 5226, which expands the guidance and adds new assignment policies.

sections.title: What Are Protocol Registries
sections.content:
Internet protocols often need to assign identifiers like port numbers, option types, algorithm codes, and MIME types. These identifiers must be unique and consistent across all implementations. To achieve this, a central authority manages each set of identifiers.

For IETF protocols, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) plays this role. However, each protocol's needs are different. Some registries can grow forever, while others have limited space. Some need approval from experts, while others allow anyone to request a number. RFC 2434 provides a framework for thinking about these issues and guidelines for documenting registry policies.
sections.eli5: A protocol might say 'I need option numbers 1 through 255.' But who decides what each number means? IANA does, but it needs written rules.

sections.title: Choosing an Assignment Policy
sections.content:
The first issue to consider is the size of the registry. A small registry (like TCP port numbers 0-65535) needs careful management to avoid exhaustion. A large or unlimited registry can be more liberal with assignments.

Another consideration is whether to delegate the registry. DNS domain names and Object Identifiers use hierarchical delegation: IANA controls the top level, and delegated managers control subdomains. This reduces the burden on IANA.

Finally, the level of review needed depends on the risk of bad assignments. Simple registries like vendor MIME types can use first-come-first-served. Registries that affect interoperability often need expert review or IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: If you have only 100 numbers to give out, you must be careful. If you have millions, you can be more generous. If mistakes are dangerous, get expert approval.

sections.title: Common Assignment Policies
sections.content:
RFC 2434 defines several example policies. Private Use allows each site to use values however it wants, with no coordination. First Come First Served allows anyone to get a number by filling out a form, with IANA making assignments without subjective review.

Expert Review requires approval by a designated expert appointed by an IETF Area Director. Specification Required means values must be documented in an RFC or other permanent reference. IETF Consensus requires consensus from the IETF community, typically through an RFC and IESG approval. Standards Action allows assignments only for Standards Track RFCs.
sections.eli5: You can pick the right rule for your registry: anyone can grab a number, or you need expert permission, or you need everyone to agree.

sections.title: What RFCs Must Document
sections.content:
If an RFC creates a registry or modifies an existing one and expects IANA to play a role, it MUST document the assignment process. The document must state clearly whether assignments need review, and if so, what the review mechanism is. It must specify whether the IANA can make assignments without review, and if so, provide sufficient guidance so IANA can do so with minimal subjectivity.

Documents should avoid naming designated experts in the RFC itself; instead, the working group should relay expert names to the IESG when submitting the RFC for approval. Documents may also specify mailing lists where proposed assignments should be discussed before review.
sections.eli5: Write down clearly: Does IANA hand out numbers by itself, or does an expert have to approve each one? If the expert approves them, who is the expert?

sections.title: Maintaining Registries Over Time
sections.content:
Once a value is assigned, some registries need updating as circumstances change. For example, MIME types can accumulate security notes, and contact information may change. RFC 2434 discusses who should be responsible for maintenance and whether registrations can be updated by their authors or require IANA or IESG approval.

In some cases, mechanisms for attaching comments to a registration allow disagreements to be documented without changing the original registration. In others, the IESG may reassign ownership of a registration if the original author cannot be reached.
sections.eli5: Once a number is assigned, people might find security problems or better information about it. Decide now who can update the registration.

sections.title: Security and Registry Integrity
sections.content:
Assignments can be security-sensitive. If an attacker can register false information about a number, or claim a number for a malicious purpose, it could affect the entire Internet. RFC 2434 notes that information creating or updating a registration needs to be authenticated, and that security descriptions in registrations must be accurate.

A statement that there are 'no security issues' for a registered value can be harmful if it is false. It is more honest to state that 'security issues have not been assessed.'
sections.eli5: Make sure the person asking for a number is really who they claim to be. And if there are security risks, say so clearly.
